key_insight: Maia-2’s weaker chess play under low-skill conditioning reflects altered use of retained knowledge rather than a measurable loss of concept knowledge.
engineering_relevance: When building skill-conditioned simulators, evaluate internal knowledge separately from output quality because weak behavior can mask stronger available capabilities.
method: Hold board positions and model weights fixed; analyze cases where skill conditioning switches predictions from blunders to best moves.
Probe internal states for 172 chess concepts and test probe transfer across skill levels.
Test knowledge recovery through output-layer-only fine-tuning and sparse-autoencoder feature steering.
evidence_signal: Concept-probe accuracy stayed nearly constant across skill conditions, while output-layer fine-tuning raised lowest-skill best-move accuracy from 14.4% to 82.8% on the studied positions.
watch_item: Findings concern selected skill-sensitive chess positions; generalization to broader gameplay or natural-language user simulation remains unestablished.
paper_title: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels
